title: Top K Frequent Elements
summary: You get a list of integers `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the `k` values that appear most often in `nums`, in any order. The answer is always unique: no two values tie for the last of the `k` places. Your solution must run faster than O(n log n) time, where n is the length of `nums`.

examples.explanation: 4 appears three times and 6 twice, while 1 and 2 appear once. [6, 4] is just as good.
3 appears three times, more than any other value.

constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ the number of distinct values in nums

approaches.twist: Count each value, then put the values into buckets indexed by count and read the buckets from the highest count down.
Count each value, then use a heap to pick the k values with the highest counts.
approaches.note: Works, and a heap of size k needs only O(n log k) time, but k can be as large as the number of distinct values, which makes it O(n log n). The target is O(n).

approaches.twist: Count each value, sort the distinct values by count from high to low, and take the first k.
approaches.note: Works, but sorting the distinct values by count takes O(n log n) time. The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: Frequency comes first: one pass with a Counter gives every value's count. What's left is picking the k biggest counts.
Sorting the counts costs O(n log n), and so does a heap when k is large. No count can exceed n, so put each value in a bucket indexed by its count and read the buckets from the top: O(n).

constraintReading: len(nums) can reach 10⁵. Counting takes one O(n) pass; picking the top k is the hard part. Sorting the counts is O(n log n), and a heap is O(n log k), just as slow when k is near the number of distinct values. Faster than O(n log n) means O(n): a count is at most n, so counts can index buckets directly.

hints.clarify: Do you return the counts or the values? The values, in any order. Try [7, 2, 7, 5, 2, 7] with k = 2 by hand: 7 appears three times, 2 twice and 5 once, so the answer is [7, 2]. What is the biggest count any value could have? At most len(nums), when every item is the same value.
hints.approach: Hash map and counting, then buckets. Count how often each value appears with a `Counter`. A count is a whole number from 1 to n, so it can be a list index: make n + 1 empty buckets and put each value in the bucket at its count. Then read the buckets from the highest count down, taking values until you have k of them. No sorting needed.
hints.whyNot: Counting is the easy part; ordering the counts is where the time goes. Sorting the distinct values by count is O(n log n), which the problem rules out. A heap of size k is O(n log k), but k can be as big as the number of distinct values, which brings it back to O(n log n). Buckets indexed by count need only O(n).

slots.setup: A `Counter` of `nums`, then a list of n + 1 empty buckets, one per possible count from 0 to n.
slots.loop: Visit each distinct value and its count once to fill the buckets; then walk the bucket indexes from n down to 1.
slots.update: Append each value to the bucket at its count, so the bucket at index c holds every value that appears exactly c times.
slots.record: Walking down from the top bucket, add each value you meet to the answer; the first values you meet are the most frequent.
slots.return: Stop and return the answer as soon as it holds k values. The problem promises no tie for the last place, so the k values are the same whichever order you read a bucket in.

solution.explanation: Counting takes one pass, O(n). There are at most n distinct values, so filling the buckets is O(n), and walking the n + 1 buckets from the top touches each bucket and each value once: O(n) time in total. The `Counter` and the buckets each hold at most n entries, so the space is O(n). `count.most_common(k)` gives the same answer in one line, but it sorts or uses a heap, so it is O(n log k) or worse.

events.label: bucket
events.say: {x} has a count of {c}, so it goes in bucket {c}

events.label: take
events.say: Bucket {c} holds {x}. No value left has a count above {c}, so take it

events.label: return
events.say: That fills all k = {k} places with the most frequent values: return {top}

predict.ask: Will this value complete the answer?

related.relation: Also sorts values into groups by a shared key, but there the key describes a word's letters, not how often a value appears.
